entries: The bulb on its back holds a store of nutrients that keeps it going when food is scarce. It is happiest in quiet, sunny meadows.
It can lash out with thin vines that sprout from beside the bulb. Trainers prize it as a first partner because it is calm, sturdy and easy to raise.
The bud on its back is heavy, and Ivysaur walks with a slow, steady gait to keep it from bumping. It rarely breaks into a run.
Ivysaur uses its vines to reach fruit hanging from high branches. It is wary of fire and keeps well away from campsites.
The great flower on its back takes years to reach its full size. Venusaur rests at the heart of the meadow while smaller Pokémon gather in its shade.
It moves slowly, held down by its own heavy frame. When threatened it plants its feet and fires bursts of energy gathered in the flower.
A small lizard whose tail ends in a flickering flame. It is curious and tags along after anything that moves, sniffing it with interest.
It prefers warm, rocky places and avoids getting caught in the rain. Charmander likes to curl up near hot stones, keeping its tail out of puddles.
Charmeleon is hot-tempered and eager to prove itself. It swipes at rivals with sharp claws and snarls when it loses.
Charmeleon grows fond only of trainers who have earned its respect. Its red scales are hot to the touch, even on cold days.
Charizard soars on broad wings high over mountains, and its roar echoes through the valleys below.
Its fiery breath can turn stone to slag. It spreads its wings wide when it wants to look as large as possible to a rival.
Squirtle naps in the sun on riverside rocks and slips into the water at the first sign of trouble.
Young Squirtle play together in shallow ponds, racing and spraying one another. They are fond of people and easy to befriend.
Wartortle's shell is a deeper blue than Squirtle's and bears the nicks of many scuffles. It can hold its breath for a long time.
When it surfaces, Wartortle often bares its teeth at onlookers, more out of pride than anger. Its tail is soft and fluffy.
Two cannons jut from Blastoise's shell, and it can turn them to point in any direction. It rarely loses its composure.
On land Blastoise walks slowly, but in water it moves with surprising grace. It rests in shallow bays with only its shell above the surface.
Caterpie wriggles along branches on its many short legs, nibbling as it goes. Its bright green body blends in with the foliage.
When threatened, Caterpie curls up and stays perfectly still. The round markings on its head look like big eyes to a hungry bird.
Metapod clings to a branch and waits without moving, sometimes for many days. A thin thread holds it in place.
Its green shell hardens to shield it while it changes. If something knocks it loose, it simply lies still where it falls.
Butterfree flutters across wide fields, resting on tall flowers. In autumn, great numbers travel together toward warmer lands.
It shakes its wings to scatter dust that can make foes drowsy or numb. Its large eyes are made up of many tiny lenses.
The pointed barb on its head carries a mild poison. It crawls through woods and fields, eating the leaves it hides beneath.
Its bright colors warn birds to stay away. Weedle are most common in thick woods, where many can be found on a single tree.
Kakuna can barely move, but it is not helpless: a barb inside its shell can jab anything that grabs it.
Kakuna hang from branches in clusters. A grove with many of them is quiet but dangerous, since Beedrill nearby will guard them fiercely.
Beedrill zips through the air at great speed and strikes with the venomous needles on its forelegs. Its wings hum loudly in flight.
Beedrill guard their hives from anything that comes near. Their bright stripes warn other creatures to keep their distance.
Pidgey would rather flee than fight, and it takes off with a flurry of wings at the first sign of trouble.
Flocks of Pidgey peck at seeds and small bugs along roadsides. They know their home area well and seldom stray far.
Pidgeotto is a skilled flyer that glides on rising warm air for long stretches. Its sharp eyes miss very little below.
It hunts small Pokémon in open fields, diving at them from a great height. Its talons are strong and sharply hooked.
Pidgeot's long crest streams behind it as it flies. It can cruise for hours above the clouds without tiring.
Its wingbeats can whip up gales strong enough to bend trees. It nests on high crags with a wide view of its hunting grounds.
Rattata scurries through grass and alleys alike, nibbling whatever it finds. It is small, quick and hard to catch.
It breeds quickly, so a single pair can soon become a whole colony. Its tail curls up when it is content.
Raticate is much bolder than Rattata and will stand up to dogs and cats. Its fangs are thick and yellow.
Raticate is fierce when cornered. It builds its nest in hidden places and guards it, biting anything that comes too close.
Spearow darts low over the grass in short, quick bursts. It quarrels noisily with other birds over the best perches.
Unlike Pidgey, it is short-tempered and bold. Spearow will chase anything that wanders near its nest, even a much larger Pokémon.
Fearow screeches loudly as it circles above its territory. Its call carries a long way over open plains.
Fearow has a long, sharp beak and a fierce temper. It will drive off birds twice its size that stray too close.
Ekans hides in tall grass, flicking its tongue to taste the air. It strikes quickly and then slips away before the target can react.
Ekans basks on warm rocks during the day. Its purple scales are smooth and glossy, and they shed in one piece.
Arbok spreads its hood to show a startling face-like design that sends smaller creatures fleeing. It can hold that pose without moving for an hour.
Arbok guards its territory jealously and hisses at anyone who comes near. Its fangs carry a venom that numbs.
Small sparks crackle along its tail whenever it is curious. A Pikachu that trusts its trainer will rest its cheek against their hand without giving the slightest jolt.
It gnaws the bark of young trees for the minerals beneath. Orchards near its nests are sometimes found with every trunk ringed by rows of tiny tooth marks.
It digs shallow dens beneath fallen logs and lines them with dry moss. The moss smoulders now and then, so its homes are easy to find by their scorched doorways.
A Raichu in a good mood gives off a faint buzz that radios nearby pick up as static. Its feelings can be read from across a field this way.
Sandshrew's yellow hide is covered in small, hard plates like bricks. It scratches grubs out of the sand with its claws.
When dust storms blow, Sandshrew curls up in its burrow and waits for calm weather. It digs with surprising speed.
Sandslash's back bristles with sharp, brown spikes. It burrows into the sand and waits there with only its spikes showing.
Its claws are long and curved, made for digging. Sandslash living in the desert are quick to anger when disturbed.
This small, gentle Pokémon prefers to stay close to its family in the grass. It nibbles on tender shoots and seeds.
Though it rarely starts a fight, the barbs along its back can deliver a nasty sting to anything that grabs it.
Nidorina is a calm and caring Pokémon that keeps watch over the younger ones in its group.
It digs burrows in soft ground and lines them with dry grass. When cornered, it lets out a high cry to call others to its side.
Nidoqueen's thick tail and sturdy legs make it hard to knock over. It lumbers about calmly unless provoked.
It leads its family through the grassland, the young following close behind. Few predators dare to challenge it.
This small Pokémon is bold and curious, poking its horn into anything new. It roams the grassland in search of food.
Males of this kind compete over who has the biggest horn. They often clash head to head in playful contests.
Nidorino storms about its territory and challenges any rival it meets. Its horn grows longer with every year.
Nidorino's ears twitch constantly, catching the slightest rustle. It sleeps lightly and wakes at once if something approaches.
Nidoking stamps across the grassland with heavy steps. Its thick purple hide is tough enough to turn aside most claws.
Its horn is sharp and coated in poison. Nidoking is protective of its family and fights fiercely for them.
It gathers smooth pebbles that sparkle under starlight and arranges them in rings on mountain ledges. Nobody has yet worked out what the patterns are meant to say.
Its steps are so light that it leaves no prints in fresh snow. Hikers often hear its soft giggling long before they spot its pink shape among the rocks.
It keeps to high, quiet slopes and sleeps curled in hollows lined with moss. A single Clefable will look after a whole circle of younger Clefairy.
Its small wings cannot lift it, yet it flaps them steadily while it keeps watch at night. The rhythm seems to soothe any Clefairy dozing nearby.
Vulpix has six curled tails and soft russet fur. It is clever and alert, and it watches strangers closely before approaching.
It shelters in caves and hollow logs when the weather turns wet. A ball of fire it spits out lights the dark around it.
Each of its nine golden tails sways gently as it walks. It is graceful and proud, and seldom lets people see it.
Many old tales tell of Ninetales leading travelers astray in misty woods. Its fur stays warm to the touch even in winter.
Jigglypuff loves to perform and will sing for anyone who stops to listen. Few manage to stay awake until the end.
Its body is soft and stretchy, and it can puff up like a balloon. It sulks when it is ignored.
Wigglytuff is gentle and loves to be hugged. Its long ears twitch with pleasure when it is stroked.
Its fluffy coat makes it a favorite cushion for napping children. It sings in a voice softer and warmer than Jigglypuff's.
Colonies of thousands cling to the ceilings of caves, packed so tightly that the rock seems to breathe. At dusk they pour out of the entrance in a single shrieking ribbon.
A Zubat tracks the warmth of other creatures through total darkness. It prefers sleeping prey, and its bite is so small that most victims never stir.
Its wide mouth takes up most of its body. It swoops through tunnels with that mouth gaping, scooping up insects and anything else that drifts past.
A Golbat will patrol the same stretch of cave every night for years. Explorers learn to recognise individuals by the notches torn in their wings.
Oddish hops about on two short feet, its leafy top bobbing as it goes. It is shy and hides when people walk past.
On clear nights it gathers with others in open fields. It grows sleepy and sluggish in dry weather.
Gloom shuffles along with its head drooping, as if it is always tired. Its round flower is heavy for its small body.
It grows dizzy in strong sunlight and prefers shaded woods. Bugs avoid the patches of ground where it lives.
Its broad red petals are heavy and droop when it is tired. It keeps its flower turned toward the light whenever it can.
It is slow-moving, so it relies on its poison to keep enemies away. It prefers warm forests where rain falls often.
Paras scuttles across the forest floor on six short legs. The two orange mushrooms riding on it get bigger as it grows.
It favors damp, shady ground where fungi thrive. When startled, it backs away slowly with its pincers raised.
The great mushroom cap on Parasect's back has grown so wide that it hides the bug underneath. Its eyes have turned a pale white.
A cloud of spores puffs from its cap whenever it is jostled. People walking in its woods cover their mouths.
Venonat's round, fuzzy body is light enough to be tossed by the wind. It hops through the undergrowth in search of food.
Its huge red eyes are made of many tiny parts. Touching its fur can leave a painful rash.
Venomoth's pale wings beat silently as it glides through the dark. It shakes loose a fine dust whenever it is alarmed.
Venomoth is nervous by nature and darts erratically through the air. It sips tree sap and nectar between hunts for smaller insects.
Diglett pops its head out of the ground to look around, then vanishes again in a flash. Its pink nose twitches as it sniffs the air.
Diglett travels in small family groups beneath fields and gardens. Nobody is sure what the rest of its body looks like.
Three heads share one body hidden beneath the ground. They pop up together and look about in three directions at once.
Dugtrio can tunnel through hard clay faster than a person can run. Some say the three heads take turns deciding where to dig.
Meowth is clever and sly, and it often hangs around markets hoping for scraps. It washes its face with its paws after every meal.
Meowth is lazy by day and active at dusk. The gold charm on its forehead is its pride, and it keeps it polished.
Persian walks with an elegant, unhurried grace, and the red gem on its forehead gleams. It is admired in many cities as a symbol of luxury.
Persian is quick and silent on its feet and stalks prey like a shadow. It purrs only for those it fully trusts.
It waddles along riverbanks, staring blankly at the current for hours. When it finally blinks, nearby fish tend to scatter as if struck by something nobody saw.
Its webbed feet make it a strong swimmer, though it rarely seems to notice it is in the water. It often drifts downstream without the least concern.
It hunts at dawn in lakes so still they mirror the sky. A Golduck waits among the reeds without a sound, watching the shallows for a careless fish.
Fishing villages once believed a Golduck by the pier meant a week of fair weather. More likely it came because the boats left scraps behind.
Mankey has a fiery temper and stamps its feet when frustrated. Its round, fluffy body bounces as it hops about.
Mankey climbs trees nimbly and leaps between branches with ease. It is fond of fruit and will pick a fight over a single berry.
Primeape glares at everything around it and punches the air when it cannot find a target. Its fists are hard as stone.
Primeape lives alone in mountain forests. Its fur bristles when it is about to lose its temper.
Growlithe is brave and devoted, and it stays close beside its trainer wherever they go. Its fluffy mane is warm to the touch.
It has a cheerful bark and a wagging tail. Growlithe is often seen keeping watch over farms and homes.
Arcanine's bark carries across whole valleys. It leaps between rocky ledges with powerful bounds and lands without a sound.
It is loyal to a single trainer for life and will bound to their side at a call. Its thick mane ripples as it runs.
A swirl shows through the skin of its belly. It waddles awkwardly on land and is far happier swimming.
Poliwag swims by wagging its broad tail. It lives in ponds and puddles, and gathers in large numbers after heavy rain.
Poliwhirl is a strong swimmer with powerful arms and enjoys wrestling with others in shallow water.
It often sits on a riverbank, watching the current go by. Its round body wobbles when it croaks.
Poliwrath has thick, powerful arms and a no-nonsense attitude. It practices its punches by striking waterfalls.
It guards the ponds where Poliwag hatch, chasing off anything that comes to cause trouble. Its swirl stands out boldly on its chest.
Its tail twitches while it dozes, as if it were dreaming of a chase. An Abra can nap anywhere, even balanced on top of a fence post.
It is often found curled in the corners of libraries and old houses. Visitors report books left lying open at a page they had just been thinking of.
Its long moustache quivers when it senses someone staring at it. It answers with a soft hum that leaves the onlooker briefly forgetting why they came.
It dislikes being moved and will find its way back to the same corner each night, however far it is carried. It sleeps sitting upright with its eyes half open.
It solves the puzzles researchers leave for it before the boxes are even opened. Its patience with slower minds, however, is famously short.
An Alakazam hovers a little above the ground while it thinks, its two spoons turning slowly in the air. When it lands, it has usually reached a decision.
It trains by gripping cliff edges and pulling itself up again and again. Its fingertips grow so tough that they can scratch lines into granite.
Young Machop wrestle one another in the shade of quarries. The winner gets the best spot for a nap, and the loser trains twice as hard the next day.
It carries timber down steep trails for mountain villages, two logs on each shoulder. It asks for nothing in return but a bowl of rice.
Machoke that work together hum a steady rhythm to keep their lifting in time. A whole crew of them can be heard from the next valley.
Each of its four arms seems to have a mind of its own in a fight, yet they work as one when it builds. A Machamp can raise a stone wall in an afternoon.
It walks with its upper arms folded across its chest. Rival Machamp settle disputes by pressing palms together until one of them gives ground.
Bellsprout sways back and forth on its thin stalk, as if dancing to music only it can hear.
It prefers hot, humid places. Bellsprout snaps up passing insects with its bell-shaped head and swallows them.
Weepinbell's wide mouth is lined with a slippery coat that makes escape hard for anything caught inside.
It prefers dim, humid forests. Its body is light and hollow, and it sways in even the faintest breeze.
Victreebel's long vine curls up from behind its head and twitches like something alive. Its leaves are broad and sharp along the edges.
Victreebel rarely moves from its chosen spot in the forest, swaying gently as it waits for a meal to come near.
Swarms of Tentacool drift into warm bays at the end of summer. Swimmers learn to watch for the faint red glints that bob just beneath the surface.
It has no bones, and its body sways with every current like a sheet of glass. Fishermen untangle them from their nets with thick gloves and gentle hands.
It drifts over reefs with its tentacles drawn up short, looking far smaller than it is. Divers keep a distance of twice their own height from one.
When the tide goes out, a Tentacruel may sit in a rock pool for hours, its crystals flickering as though it were signalling to others far away.
It basks on sunny ledges to warm its stony body before climbing. A cold Geodude moves so slowly that moss can take root on its back.
Its two arms end in knuckles that wear down over the years and grow back thicker after every winter. Old Geodude have fists twice the size of young ones.
It slams its fists down together to split boulders apart, and the crack echoes along the valley. Quarry workers have learned to wait for a Graveler before they lay charges.
On cold nights Graveler huddle together on ridgelines. In the morning they look like a heap of loose scree until they stretch and rumble apart.
Its rocky shell takes its colour from the minerals it eats, so Golem from different mountains wear different hues. Collectors compare the patterns on old fragments.
Golem settle on the same mountainside for decades. When one finally moves, the whole slope shifts with it, and new paths open up where it has been.
A Ponyta's hooves leave small scorched crescents in the grass wherever it trots. Herds are easy to follow across the plains by these little burnt prints.
Its fiery mane burns brighter when it is happy. Ranchers once kept a herd of Ponyta to hold off the frost from their fields on cold spring nights.
A Rapidash races from horizon to horizon in a straight line, leaving a trail of singed grass. It slows down only when it reaches water.
It is proud and refuses any rider who has not earned its trust. Those it accepts say the heat of its mane is gentle, like a summer evening.
Slowpoke yawns often and moves at its own easy pace. Nothing seems to hurry it, not even a storm.
Its pink tail is long and thick, and it drips with water when it comes ashore. It often naps with its mouth hanging open.
A Shellder bit its tail and has stayed attached ever since. The poison from the bite has made it even dreamier.
Slowbro wanders the shore in a happy daze. The weight hanging from its tail makes it walk upright, swaying with each step.
Its screws loosen when it runs low on charge, and it wobbles as it drifts. A quick visit to a wall socket tightens it right back up.
It is drawn to anything made of steel. Workshops keep their doors shut, or they find their tools stuck to the ceiling in the morning.
Its three linked bodies spin in turn while it floats, and radios crackle wherever it passes. Engineers have measured its field reaching across an entire street.
It nests in the rafters of power stations, humming in step with the generators. Workers there count it a lucky omen and leave it alone.
Farfetch'd is never seen without its green stalk, which it treats as its most precious possession. It strikes a proud pose when challenged.
Farfetch'd keeps its feathers neatly preened and its stalk in good condition. It gets flustered when either is ruffled.
Doduo cannot fly, but its long, sturdy legs let it run very quickly across open ground.
The two heads seldom agree on which way to go, and it wobbles about as each pulls in its own direction.
Its three heads give it a wide view of its surroundings, so it is almost impossible to sneak up on. It races across plains on powerful legs.
The heads sometimes squabble among themselves over food. When all three cry out together, the noise can be heard far across the grassland.
Seel loves the cold and naps on drifting floes. It claps its flippers together when it is excited.
Its thick fur and layer of fat protect it from the cold. Seel is playful and often follows boats along icy coastlines.
Dewgong's sleek white body slips through icy water with barely a ripple. Its tail fin is broad and strong.
Dewgong is a gentle Pokémon that sometimes guides lost swimmers to land. It stays comfortable in water that is below freezing.
Grimer's body is a lump of purple goo that changes shape as it moves. It leaves a slimy trail wherever it crawls.
Grimer feeds on waste and grows bigger as it eats. It is so sticky that touching it can leave a stench on the skin for days.
Muk is a heaving mass of sludge that slowly spreads wherever it settles. Flies swarm around it day and night.
Muk smells so bad that people feel faint near it. It lies in still pools of waste, barely moving for days.
Shellder rests on sandy seabeds with its shell slightly open, its long tongue lolling out. It snaps shut at the first hint of danger.
Shellder sometimes latches onto other Pokémon and refuses to let go. It feeds on tiny scraps that drift by in the current.
Cloyster's shell is ringed with sharp spikes and is darkly glossy. It lies on the seabed and filters seawater to catch tiny food.
It lives in cold seas, where its spikes are often coated in a thin crust of ice. Divers give it plenty of room.
Its body is a thin cloud that thickens on damp nights. A Gastly that drifts into a room leaves the windows fogged with patterns that look like faces.
It giggles as it slips through keyholes. Old houses with a Gastly in residence are said to smell faintly of burnt matches.
Its gloved hands float apart from its body, and it uses them to tap on windows at midnight. It seems to relish the startled faces that peer out.
Haunter follow travellers through dark woods, keeping exactly one step behind. Turn around, and it has already slipped into the nearest shadow.
It grins constantly, even in its sleep. When a Gengar laughs, every candle in the room gutters at once and then flares up blue.
A Gengar sometimes sits at the foot of a sleeper's bed all night, perfectly still. In the morning the sleeper recalls dreams that were not their own.
Its tunnels can run for miles under a mountain, and many old mines began as Onix burrows widened by hand. The walls are polished smooth by its body.
The boulders of its body grind together with a low groan as it moves. Villages above its tunnels feel their floors tremble in the night.
It feeds on the dreams of sleeping creatures, which it seeks out at night. Its long nose twitches when it senses a sweet dream nearby.
By day it ambles about in a drowsy daze. Its mild psychic power lets it make those it meets feel tired.
Hypno carries a gleaming pendulum on a string wherever it goes. Old stories warn children never to follow it.
Hypno's thick white mane bristles as it focuses its mind. It prefers to act at dusk, when shadows grow long.
Krabby's two big pincers make up a good part of its weight. It waves them in the air to look larger when threatened.
Krabby scuttles sideways across the sand and ducks into the surf when danger comes. It nips at anything that steps too close.
Kingler's huge claw can crush steel. Rivals size each other up by comparing claws, and the smaller one usually backs down.
Kingler lives along rocky shores and in river mouths. It snaps its claw shut with a loud crack to warn away intruders.
Voltorb's round body is smooth and shiny, and it hums softly when charged. It rolls to get about.
Voltorb dislikes being touched and may let off a sharp crackle of static. It gathers in places where electric current hums in the walls.
Electrode wears a wide grin and rolls about at alarming speed. It bounces off walls without slowing down.
It is drawn to places thick with electricity and grows restless during thunderstorms. Workers at power stations keep a careful eye on it.
Exeggcute is six pink seeds that cling together, each with its own little face. They chatter among themselves in faint squeaks.
When one of the six cracks, the others crowd around it until it mends. They nest near tropical trees.
Exeggutor's three heads often argue among themselves about where to go. It settles the matter by walking toward the sun.
It stands as tall as a palm tree and sways in sea breezes. Its psychic powers grow sharper in the heat of the day.
Cubone wears a hard skull over its head like a helmet, and peers out through its eyeholes. It is shy and keeps to itself.
It carries a bone club and swings it at anything that startles it. Cubone that find a caring trainer slowly come out of their shells.
Marowak wields its bone club with great skill, swinging it hard and fast. The bone grows harder through years of battle.
Having outgrown its shyness, it faces danger head on. It keeps a collection of bones in its den and guards them closely.
Hitmonlee's legs coil like springs and lash out with blinding speed. Few foes see the kick coming.
Hitmonlee trains alone, polishing its techniques for hours on end. It keeps its balance perfectly on just one foot.
Hitmonchan bobs and weaves on light feet, slipping past blows before striking back. It wraps its fists in tough padding.
Hitmonchan keeps its arms raised to guard at all times. It can wear down even stronger foes with steady, patient jabs.
Its long tongue lies coiled inside its mouth like a rope when it is not in use. A Lickitung that yawns unrolls it all the way to the ground.
Its tail thumps the ground in time with its chewing. A Lickitung that has found a patch of ripe berries can be heard from far away.
Koffing drifts lazily through the air, bumping into things as it goes. The craters on its skin puff out little clouds of smoke.
Koffing grows bloated after a meal of fumes. People living near it keep their windows shut tight.
Weezing's two heads drift side by side, one large and one small. They seldom bother each other and seem content together.
Weezing hovers over trash heaps, breathing in the stench of decay as if it were a feast. It avoids clean, fresh air.
It wallows in dry dust to keep pests off its hide, and a herd raises a cloud that can be seen for miles. It sleeps standing, its head held low.
Its armoured hide is scarred by every rock it has ever run into. Older Rhyhorn are almost entirely covered in pale, criss-crossing lines.
It rests in the shade of cliffs through the hottest part of the day and works through the night. Hillsides near its range are riddled with round, deep holes.
It plants its tail like a third leg before it swings its arms. Rocks it strikes this way burst apart in a single blow.
The pouch on its belly is soft and deep, and Chansey often tuck small treasures into it beside the egg. A ribbon or a smooth stone may stay there for years.
Chansey hum quietly to themselves while they work, a tune that seems to calm frightened patients. Nurses say that each Chansey has a hum of its own.
A Tangela left under a tree overnight is often found in the morning tied loosely to the trunk. It seems to grip whatever it leans on while it sleeps.
It likes to sun itself on warm stones by the roadside. Passers-by take it for a heap of cut weeds until two eyes blink out of the blue mass.
Kangaskhan is a devoted parent and teaches its young to forage as soon as it can walk. It is calm unless its family is threatened.
Kangaskhan travels slowly across grassy plains, grazing as it goes. The little one peeks out of the pouch to watch the world.
Horsea squirts dark ink when frightened, then darts away to hide among the coral. Its snout is long and narrow.
Horsea lives in calm, warm seas. Its little fin beats quickly to keep it steady in the current.
Sharp spines run along its back and carry poison. Swimmers who brush against one may feel faint.
Seadra spins its body to churn up the water and confuse its foes. It is short-tempered and stings without warning.
Its bright fins flash orange and white as it turns, so anglers can spot one from the bank. A Goldeen on a line fights far harder than its size suggests.
It spends the cold months resting in deep pools beneath the ice, barely moving its fins. In spring it is thin and very hungry.
It patrols a single bend of a river all its life. Children who swim there often say it seems to know them and keeps a polite distance.
Its colours are brightest on the first warm days of the year. An old Seaking's fins grow ragged at the edges, but it still swims with stately grace.
Staryu's red core blinks in a slow, steady rhythm. It clings to rocks in tide pools when the sea goes out.
Staryu spins its body to swim through water. It is a curious creature and often drifts toward boats.
Starmie's jewel-like core is set in two layers of stiff, star-shaped arms. It drifts through the sea alone and seldom gathers with others.
Nobody knows where Starmie first came from, and some people think it fell from the night sky. It sends out pulses of light no one has decoded.
It rehearses its routines in front of puddles to watch its reflection. A Mr. Mime that has been applauded will repeat the same gesture all afternoon.
It bows deeply to anyone who watches it, then waits for them to bow back. Ignoring the courtesy seems to hurt its feelings for days.
It leaves its mark on the trunks of trees at the edges of its range, three deep slashes in a row. Rivals that find the marks seldom cross them.
It barely makes a sound as it moves. The first sign of a Scyther is often a falling twig, sliced so cleanly that its end shines.
Jynx has a long golden mane that it tosses as it walks. Its gaze is calm and a little haughty.
Jynx prefers cold places and makes its home in icy lands. Its lips are its pride, and it uses them to deliver a freezing kiss.
It paces back and forth when restless, and the air around it starts to smell like rain. Animals nearby grow skittish long before the first spark.
Its striped fur stands on end while it charges up. A fully charged Electabuzz looks almost twice its true size and gives off a steady drone.
It lounges in hot springs at the foot of volcanoes, and the water boils around it. Locals cook eggs in those pools whenever it looks the other way.
Its breath leaves trails of shimmering air. An angry Magmar glows white along its lips and can scorch a wooden door with a single sigh.
Pinsir clacks its two great horns together to warn rivals away. It is short-tempered and battles any bug that comes near.
Rows of spikes line the inside of its horns, so whatever they catch cannot wriggle loose. It feeds on tree sap.
Tauros snorts and stamps the ground before every charge. Its horns are thick and curved, and its hide is tough as leather.
Tauros lives in herds on open plains. The bulls clash horns to decide which of them will lead the group.
A Magikarp's whiskers are surprisingly sensitive and twitch at the faintest current. It uses them to find the slow, quiet pools where it likes to drift.
Scale patterns differ from one Magikarp to the next, and anglers who keep records can tell which fish they have landed before. Some catch the same one dozens of times.
Once it settles in a lake, other large creatures move away. Its bellow carries for miles across open water on calm nights.
A Gyarados will circle a sunken wreck for years, guarding it as its own. Divers who come too close return with stories of a shadow as long as the hull.
Lapras glides across calm seas with its long neck held high. Its broad shell is smooth and wide.
Lapras is clever and calm, and it remembers the faces of those who have treated it kindly. It enjoys swimming alongside ships.
Left alone, Ditto settles into a lazy purple puddle with a simple face. It can stay that way for days, quite content.
Ditto is found in many places, often near Pokémon it can imitate. Two Ditto meeting each other struggle to decide which shape to take.
It is quick to make friends and often follows people home on its own. Its thick ruff fluffs up in cold weather and lies flat when it feels safe.
It loves to burrow into laundry baskets and warm blankets. When it finally pokes its head out, its ears twitch at every sound in the house.
Its long tail fin drives it through rivers in graceful arcs. On land it moves with a lazy, rolling walk and stops often to drink.
It keeps the ponds it lives in clear by eating the algae that clouds them. Gardeners with lily ponds welcome a visiting Vaporeon gladly.
It calms itself after a fright by running long loops across the grass until the crackle in its coat dies down. A Jolteon at rest still hums faintly.
A Jolteon is hard to pet, because every touch gives a little snap. Those who live with one keep their hands damp and their metal jewellery off.
It loves to curl up in front of fireplaces, though it is far warmer than any hearth. Its fluffy collar stays soft even after a long nap in the coals.
Flareon shake out their fur in winter to keep snow from settling on them. Flakes falling around one turn to drizzle before they land.
It moves in short, jerky steps as if checking each one before taking it. Its colours flicker slightly while it works out something it has never met before.
A Porygon left alone will sort any objects nearby by size and shape. Its owners joke that it cannot rest while anything is out of place.
Omanyte's spiral shell is ridged and pale blue. It drifted through warm ancient seas, feeding on plankton and tiny creatures.
Researchers revive Omanyte from fossils found in old seabeds. In tanks, it bobs gently and waves its tentacles at visitors.
Omastar's mouth is ringed by a sharp beak strong enough to crack open shellfish. It crept across the ancient seafloor in search of them.
Omastar was a fierce hunter of ancient seas. Fossils of it are often found in layers of old seabed rock.
Kabuto scuttled along ancient seashores hiding beneath its hard shell. Its glowing eyes peered out to spot food in the dark.
Kabuto molts its shell as it grows, and the old shells are sometimes found buried in sand.
Kabutops has scythes for arms and a hard, smooth carapace. It struck quickly from shadowy waters long ago.
Fossils show Kabutops crouched in the shallows of ancient bays. Revived ones are restless and pace their tanks at night.
Aerodactyl's leathery wings carry it swiftly on high winds. Its jaws are lined with jagged teeth, and its temper is short.
Aerodactyl screeches loudly as it swoops down on prey. It is thought to have hunted from cliffs high above the sea.
It wakes only when its nose catches something to eat. Then it rises slowly, follows the smell in a straight line and returns to the same spot to sleep again.
A wild Snorlax shifts position just once a day, rolling over with a groan heard across the valley. Moss grows in the shadow of its back.
A legendary bird with long, flowing blue tail feathers. It lives alone on remote, frozen peaks and is rarely seen.
As Articuno flies, it leaves sparkling trails of ice crystals behind it. Travelers tell tales of glimpsing its blue plumage in blizzards.
Bolts of lightning crackle around this legendary bird as it flies. It is drawn to places where storms are raging.
The crackle of its feathers can be heard long before it comes into view. Its cry sounds like a peal of thunder.
A legendary bird with a crest and tail of living flame. The sky around it glows orange as it passes overhead.
Moltres makes its home among volcanic peaks. Those who glimpse it say the air around it shimmers with heat.
Dratini keeps out of sight in deep, clear water and is seldom seen. Its smooth blue body is surprisingly long for its weight.
Its body gives off a gentle energy. Fishermen who caught one long ago spoke of a slender blue serpent with a white snout.
Dragonair's long body glides through the air without wings, rippling like a ribbon. Its eyes are calm and gentle.
Dragonair lives in pure lakes and seas, far from people. Its long white horn and blue scales shimmer in clear water.
A kindly giant that flies over the sea on surprisingly small wings. Children who meet one often find it eager to play.
Dragonite is slow to anger, but when it finally loses its temper it can flatten everything around it.
A Pokémon made by people who altered the genes of another. It possesses enormous psychic power and a fierce, wary nature.
Mewtwo rarely shows itself and prefers to stay hidden in caves. Its mind is said to be among the most powerful of any Pokémon.
Mew is playful and curious, and it tumbles through the air as if gravity meant nothing to it. Its long, thin tail helps it steer.
Mew lives in remote jungles where few people ever go. Some researchers believe many kinds of Pokémon descended from it.
The large leaf on its head turns to follow the light. Chikorita is gentle and gets along well with other Pokémon.
It often runs in circles in sunny fields, playing with others. When annoyed it swats with its big head leaf.
Bayleef is affectionate and likes to stay close to those it cares for, nudging them with its head.
It runs about on strong legs and enjoys long walks. Its neck stretches out when it reaches toward sunny spots.
Meganium walks slowly through meadows, and small Pokémon follow it for company. The bloom around its neck opens wide on sunny days.
Meganium is kind and takes care of injured Pokémon it finds in the wild. Its long stamens wave gently in the breeze.
Cyndaquil is shy and easily startled, and it often hides behind its trainer's legs. It sniffs the air constantly with its pointed nose.
It keeps the flames on its back hidden when relaxed. It loves warm places and sleeps curled up near the hearth.
Quilava's flames flare out from its neck and rump in bright collars. It is restless and seldom sits still for long.
Quilava runs at a low crouch, its fire streaming behind it. It grows bolder and more outgoing as it gains experience.
Typhlosion's fiery collar roars higher whenever it is angered. Its fur is thick and dark along its back.
Typhlosion is a calm Pokémon until provoked. Its fiery mane can scorch everything nearby in an instant.
Totodile is small but full of energy, and it charges at anything new to get a closer look. It loves splashing in puddles.
It hops and sways in a cheerful little dance when happy. In water it paddles strongly with its short limbs.
Croconaw lunges from the water with its mouth wide open. The spines on its back stand up when it is ready to fight.
It waits in rivers for prey to come close. It is quick to anger and splashes water at anything that annoys it.
On land it walks upright, swinging its heavy tail for balance. Its huge jaws can crush rock with a single bite.
Feraligatr lurks in deep rivers with only its eyes above the surface. When prey comes near, it surges out with a roar.
Sentret sits upright on its thick striped tail, which is longer than its body. It chatters nervously when it is unsure.
It builds its home in burrows with many tunnels. Young Sentret learn to stand upright almost as soon as they can walk.
Furret is quick and playful, bounding along in long, rippling leaps. Its stripes help it blend into tall grass.
Furret curls its long body around its young to keep them warm while they sleep. Its fur is soft and thick.
It perches on low branches at the edge of clearings and tilts its round head at every rustle. Its soft cooing is the first sound many campers hear after dark.
A Hoothoot fluffs its feathers into a near-perfect ball when the night turns cold. Pairs share a single hollow and take turns keeping watch.
It hunts from the highest branch of a tall pine, watching the forest floor for the slightest movement. Its catch is carried back to the same branch every time.
The pattern on its face resembles a pair of open books, and old tales made it a keeper of forest lore. It is in fact an excellent judge of its territory's every path.
Ledyba is timid and feels safe only with many others of its kind. A swarm flutters through the woods at dawn, glinting red.
Its five spots are bright on a healthy Ledyba. It flies clumsily and often lands on flowers to rest its small wings.
Ledian is most active on clear nights and rests by day under broad leaves. Its four arms let it throw punches in quick flurries.
When it is brave enough to fight alone, it shows its true strength. It wraps itself in its wings to sleep.
Spinarak hangs from a single strand in the shade of leaves. The markings on its back look like a scowling face and startle birds.
The thread it spins is tough, and people have used it to make fabric. It hunts mostly at night.
Ariados creeps along on long, striped legs and moves surprisingly fast. The horn on its head can deliver a painful jab.
Its webs are wide and strong enough to hold a small bird. It is most active late at night.
It roosts in the deepest chambers of caves, far from any light. Its purple wings fold so neatly that a sleeping Crobat looks like a small leather pouch.
A Crobat spends far more time on the wing than resting. It sleeps hanging from a single claw, its wings folded like a closed umbrella.
Chinchou's round blue body is tipped with two bobbing antennae. It gives a sharp jolt to anything that grabs it.
Chinchou rises closer to the surface on dark nights. Fishermen sometimes spot its lights twinkling beneath the waves.
Lanturn's two glowing lures dangle above its face as it swims. Curious fish swim toward them, which is exactly what it wants.
Lanturn cruises slowly through the deep, its round body bobbing as it swims. It can live comfortably at great depths.
Its ears are larger than its head and turn toward every sound. A Pichu that hears thunder in the distance sits up straight and squeaks with excitement.
Groups of Pichu play tag around the roots of old trees. When one finally gets tired, the others pile on top of it and fall asleep together.
It is often found sitting alone on rocky outcrops, gazing upward at night. Its round body rolls easily, so it wedges itself into cracks before it dozes off.
A Cleffa's laughter is said to make wilted flowers lift their heads. It hums softly to itself whenever it finds something that sparkles.
Igglybuff is round, pink and light as a feather. It giggles and wiggles whenever it is picked up.
It is fond of its trainer and follows them happily. Its round eyes sparkle when it is pleased.
It sways from side to side as it toddles about, kept upright by the weight of its shell. A Togepi that tips over waits patiently for someone to set it right.
The coloured marks on its shell are different on every Togepi. Breeders sketch them down, since they stay the same even after it evolves.
It flutters from village to village and seldom stays long in one place. Children build little perches of twigs on windowsills in the hope that one will stop by.
Its small wings beat slowly, yet it can hover for hours with no sign of tiring. A Togetic sleeps wrapped in its own wings like a small white parcel.
Natu has short wings and a bright red crest. It is light enough to perch on the thinnest twig.
Natu is silent and watchful, and it seems to sense trouble before it arrives. It is said to know what others are thinking.
Xatu's wings are marked with bold patterns of red, white and black. It folds them close like a cloak when it rests.
In some lands it is honored as a guardian of the village. People say it knows of storms long before they arrive.
Mareep is gentle and timid, and it bleats softly when it wants attention. Its fleece is thick and very fluffy.
Farmers raise Mareep in pastures and spin its wool into warm cloth. A sweater made from it crackles faintly in dry weather.
Flaaffy walks upright on two legs, and a bright orb hangs from the end of its tail. Its fleece covers only its head and middle now.
Flaaffy is gentle with people who treat it well, and it is often kept on farms to guard flocks of Mareep.
Ampharos has smooth yellow skin and a calm, kindly face. A famous lighthouse in Johto is lit by one.
Ampharos has shed all of its wool. Electricity collects in the glowing red balls on its brow and tail.
Its petals are glossy and bright, and the flowers on its head open wider in clear weather. It is cheerful and friendly.
Bellossom's flowers smell faintly sweet after a rain. Its leafy skirt rustles softly when it moves.
It plays in shallow streams by floating on its back and paddling with its round tail. A Marill can spend a whole afternoon spinning slowly in an eddy.
Groups of Marill line up along riverbanks to sun themselves after a swim. Their round blue bodies look like a row of beach balls left out to dry.
It dives to the bottom of clear lakes to graze on water plants, its long ears folded flat against its head. It surfaces with a mouthful of green every few minutes.
An Azumarill blows a fountain of spray from its nose each time it comes up for air. On calm lakes, the little plumes show exactly where it is feeding.
It plants itself beside roads and holds perfectly still for hours. Birds that perch on its arms are startled when the branch begins to sway on its own.
When it is sure nobody is watching, it shuffles a few steps to a sunnier spot. Gardeners have puzzled for years over trees that seem to move overnight.
Politoed sits on a sunny rock by the pond with its curl standing proudly. It hops with surprising height on its springy legs.
On rainy evenings it croaks for hours, and its voice carries a long way across fields and marshes.
Hoppip weighs almost nothing and drifts on the breeze like a leaf. On calm days it stays close to the ground, sunbathing.
The leaves on its head spin to steer as it floats. Children love to chase it across fields in spring.
Skiploom's yellow flower is its pride, and it turns its face toward the sky wherever it goes. It rests on rooftops and fences, waiting for a breeze.
Groups of Skiploom drift slowly across the countryside in summer. Farmers welcome them, since their visits come with fair weather.
Jumpluff's three cotton puffs are soft and almost weightless. It steers by tilting them into the wind.
In autumn, people sometimes find its loose fluff caught in the branches of tall trees. The fluff carries its spores.
Its curious hands snatch hats, bags and anything else left unattended. An Aipom that has stolen something waves it about from a high branch to show it off.
Aipom troops gather at riverbanks in the late afternoon to groom one another. Their chatter is so lively that it can be heard from the far bank.
Sunkern looks like a large seed with a single leaf sprouting from its top. It is weak and often hides under taller plants.
It is often found in fields where sunflowers grow. In a year of good weather, many of them appear across the meadows.
Sunflora's broad face is ringed with golden petals, and it smiles at anyone who passes. It waves its leafy arms in greeting.
In hot regions many gather in fields, all facing the same way. It feels limp on cloudy days.
Its wings beat so fast that they shimmer like heat haze over the water. Reeds bend flat in a circle beneath a Yanma that hangs above them.
A Yanma hatches near water and returns to the same pond every summer. Old ponds may host dozens of them, each guarding a single reed.
Its feelers twitch as it searches the soft mud for worms. A Wooper digging for food leaves a trail of tiny round holes along the bank.
A Wooper's smile never changes, whatever it is doing. It seems unbothered by almost anything, even when another Pokémon tries to chase it off.
It digs wide burrows in the clay of riverbanks and lines them with smooth stones. Families of Quagsire share the same burrow for generations.
Fishermen sometimes find one sitting beside them on the pier, watching their lines with mild interest. It never seems to want the catch, only the company.
Its forked tail sways in a slow figure of eight when it is content. Espeon groom their coats with great care, and a single tangle will keep one busy for an hour.
An Espeon basks in direct sunlight for hours, eyes half closed. Its coat seems to soak up the warmth, and it glows faintly long after sunset.
It hunts along walls and rooftops at night, moving from shadow to shadow. Small Pokémon scatter from the alleys whenever an Umbreon passes.
An Umbreon is fiercely loyal and slow to warm to strangers. It will follow its trainer home at a distance, watching every alley they pass.
It gathers in noisy flocks at dusk and roosts in bare trees on the edge of town. Their harsh cries fill the evening air until the last light fades.
A Murkrow will trade favours with other Murkrow, swapping berries for safe places to sleep. Its feathers shine with a faint purple sheen in the moonlight.
The Shellder clamped to its head is shaped like a crown. Slowking spends its days thinking about questions no one else would ask.
Other Slowpoke often gather near Slowking and seem to follow its lead. It speaks to them in low, slow murmurs.
It drifts through abandoned buildings, humming a tune that seems to come from every direction at once. Its beads clink softly as it moves.
A Misdreavus is mischievous rather than cruel. It hides small objects around a house and seems delighted when someone spends all evening hunting for them.
Each Unown holds a single shape all its life. When many gather in one place, they slowly drift into patterns that scholars still argue over.
An Unown floats almost without moving, its single eye slowly turning. Lone ones are rare, and a single sighting usually means many more are hiding nearby.
Wobbuffet is endlessly patient and will stand in one place for hours without complaint. It salutes with one arm when it is ready.
Wobbuffet's body is soft and rubbery, and blows seem to bounce right off it. It lives in quiet caves.
It stretches its long neck to reach the tender shoots at the tops of trees. Herds on the plains move slowly, stopping wherever the canopy is greenest.
It grazes on the leaves of tall trees on the open plains. When the tail is hungry it nibbles grass, and the front head pretends not to notice.
Pineco's shell is made of overlapping scales like a cone. It keeps its tiny face hidden in the gap between them.
When it feels threatened, its shell can burst open with a loud bang. It lives in forests of tall conifers.
Forretress is wrapped in a heavy shell of steel-gray plates. The shell is so dense that it weighs more than a hundred kilograms.
Forretress seldom wanders far and spends long stretches sitting perfectly still. When it opens up, sharp spikes poke out to ward off foes.
Dunsparce has a pale yellow body with blue stripes and tiny wings. It wriggles along the ground like a snake.
Few people have spotted one, since it keeps to dim, quiet places. Its stubby wings flutter when it is nervous.
It nests in cracks high on sheer cliffs, where nothing that walks can reach it. Its pale membranes catch the wind like small kites when it leaves.
A Gligar's pincers grip so firmly that it can hang from a single claw through a storm. It tucks its tail under its body to keep warm.
It sleeps coiled around a stone pillar deep underground, and in time the pillar is polished like a mirror. Miners treat such pillars with great respect.
An old Steelix moves slowly and rests for weeks between journeys. Its shining coils are sometimes mistaken for a buried iron rail.
Snubbull has a wide jaw and a gruff little growl. Despite its looks it loves to be petted and fussed over.
Snubbull is often kept as a pet in towns. It hates being alone and sulks if it is ignored.
Its huge lower fangs make it look fierce, yet it is loyal to those it trusts. Many Granbull guard homes in towns.
Its jaw is very strong, and it can bite through thick wood. It prefers to frighten foes away with a deep growl.
Qwilfish swells up into a spiky ball whenever it is alarmed. Its round eyes give it a permanently surprised look.
Its toxic spines can make a person ill for days. Fishermen handle it carefully when it ends up in their nets.
Its steel shell rings like a bell when struck, and it uses the sound to warn others away. A dented Scizor rests for days while the metal hardens again.
Its pincers snap with a sharp ring that echoes across open fields. Rivals often back down after hearing a single clap.
Shuckle's red shell is dotted with holes, and its yellow limbs poke out through them. It moves very slowly.
Its shell is hard enough to protect it from almost any blow. It spends long days tucked into crevices among sea rocks.
Its claws grip bark so firmly that it can sleep upright on a trunk through a gale. Children hunt for the deep scratches it leaves on the bark.
It is peaceful by nature and spends whole days on the same tree trunk. Only a rival intruding on its favourite tree will make it raise its horn.
It leaps between icy rocks on silent paws and leaves no tracks behind. Its red head feathers are the only flash of colour in the snow.
A Sneasel will hide food in the cracks of glaciers and remember dozens of spots. Thieves of its own kind are chased off with furious hisses.
The crescent mark on its forehead shines like a little moon. It wanders the woods snacking on sweet berries and nectar.
It looks cuddly, but it scratches hard if anything tries to take its food. Mothers keep their cubs close as they forage.
The ring-shaped mark on Ursaring's chest stands out against its brown fur. It rips into hollow logs with its massive claws to reach grubs.
Ursaring hibernates through the coldest months. Before sleeping, it eats huge amounts to build up fat.
Slugma creeps through volcanic areas at a slow, steady crawl, leaving the ground scorched behind it.
Slugma's body is so hot that it can set dry grass on fire. It dislikes rain and hides in rocky hollows when clouds gather.
Magcargo carries a lumpy shell of cooled magma on its back. Its whole body is hot enough to melt snow it touches in moments.
Magcargo lives in volcanic craters and moves slowly through the heat. Rain falling on it turns instantly into steam.
Its shaggy coat keeps it warm in freezing caves, and it sleeps buried to the eyes in snowdrifts. Only its pink snout pokes out to breathe.
Young Swinub follow their elders through the snow in a line, nose to tail. One that falls behind squeals until the others stop and wait.
It stamps on the ice ahead to judge how thick it is before crossing. A Piloswine that hears a crack turns back at once and finds another way.
A herd of Piloswine walks in single file through deep snow, each stepping in the tracks of the one ahead. The leader changes every few hours.
Corsola clusters in warm, shallow reefs, where groups of them form colorful beds. Small fish dart in and out among their branches.
Corsola moves slowly along the seabed on stubby legs. When frightened, it pulls back into a crack in the reef.
It drifts beneath rafts of floating seaweed in large schools, and the whole school turns at once at the faintest shadow overhead.
A Remoraid's fins flutter rapidly to keep it steady in rough currents. It can hang in one spot even while waves crash overhead.
It decorates the rock around its den with bits of shell and coloured glass. Divers recognise each Octillery by the patterns it has made.
An Octillery is clever with its tentacles and can open shells that other Pokémon cannot. It sometimes carries a favourite stone with it from den to den.
Delibird is a cheerful bird of snowy mountains with a sack-like tail. It hops along icy ledges rather than flying.
Delibird sometimes leaves gifts for those who have treated it kindly. It nests in sheltered hollows among the rocks.
It glides through calm seas with slow beats of its wide fins, its shadow sliding over the sandy bottom. Fish below dart for cover as it passes.
A Mantine can travel for days without resting by riding warm currents. Sailors take its broad, dark shape as a sign that the weather will hold.
Skarmory's feathers are edged like blades of steel and ring when they clash. Its red-lined wings flash in sunlight.
Skarmory nests high on cliffs, out of reach of other Pokémon. Its cry is harsh and metallic.
It marks the borders of its range with scorch marks on rocks. Travellers in the hills learn to read those black smudges as a warning.
Its breath smells of soot, and wisps of smoke curl from its nose on cold mornings. Young Houndour play by chasing each other's tails through the scrub.
It dens in hollows under rocky ledges, and the stone there is blackened from years of its breath. Its paws are tough enough to cross hot embers.
It keeps its embers banked low while resting, so only a dull red glow shows between its teeth. A sudden flare means it has caught a scent.
Kingdra is a proud dragon of the sea with a long, curled tail. It moves with great power through the water.
Its scales are smooth and tough. Sailors who glimpse it consider the sight a sign of good fortune.
Phanpy loves to play in muddy rivers, and it rolls about on the banks until it is covered in mud.
Young Phanpy follow their parents in a line, each holding the tail in front with its trunk. They squeal when separated.
Donphan's gray hide is thick and rough, like a suit of armor. It digs for roots with its tusks.
Herds of Donphan travel across dry plains in search of water. They rest together in the shade at midday.
Its rebuilt body is smoother and rounder than its first form's, and it bobs gently as it floats. Its eyes follow movement with a faint whirr.
A Porygon2 sometimes freezes for a moment, as if thinking. It hums with a soft electronic tone while it sorts through what it has learned.
Stantler's antlers curve back into rings, and a dark orb sits in each one. It lowers its head and stares when it feels uneasy.
Stantler lives in herds in quiet woods and meadows. It is wary and bolts at any unusual noise.
Smeargle loves to draw and dabs its tail across rocks and walls. Each one paints in its own style.
It is curious and studies other Pokémon closely, copying what they do. Its tail fluid changes color with its mood.
Tyrogue picks scuffles with anything it meets just to test itself. Its style of fighting changes as it learns, deciding what it will become.
Tyrogue is small but scrappy, and it hates sitting still. It is often found in gyms and dojos where people train.
Hitmontop balances upside down on the horn on its head, with its legs pointed at the sky. It practices for hours.
Its head horn is worn smooth from all its spinning. It is calm and focused outside of battle.
Smoochum hums little tunes as it wanders through the snow. It prefers cold places and avoids the heat.
Its lips are cold to the touch and can numb whatever they press. It is fond of people who play gently with it.
It loves to touch electrical outlets and plugs, giggling at every spark. Households with an Elekid keep their sockets covered.
The plug-shaped horns on its head crackle when it is excited. Two Elekid that meet will touch horns, trading a quick snap of sparks by way of greeting.
Its body is warm enough to melt snow around it in a wide circle. Magby often curl up near hot rocks and sleep through cold nights.
A Magby chases its own sparks across the ground until it trips over its feet. It sulks for a moment, then starts the chase all over again.
Miltank is a steady, good-natured Pokémon that farmers have kept for generations. It hums contentedly while grazing.
When it feels threatened, Miltank tucks itself into a ball and rolls into foes at speed. Its pink hide is thick.
Its soft fur muffles every sound, so its arrival is felt more than heard. Patients say a room grows warmer the moment a Blissey walks in.
A Blissey lines the pouch on its belly with fresh fluff every spring. The old fluff is gathered by Pokémon Centers to stuff their pillows.
Raikou bounds across the land in great leaps, gone before the eye can follow. Storms seem to gather wherever it pauses.
The cloud-like mane on its back crackles with static. Old stories tie its first appearance to a tower that burned.
Entei roams the land without rest, and the air around it shimmers with heat. Its eyes burn with a fierce, steady light.
Legends tie its birth to a great fire. Flames that it breathes are hotter than molten rock.
Suicune moves with quiet grace, its flowing tails trailing behind it like ribbons. It appears briefly and then is gone.
It is drawn to clear lakes and springs and lingers at their edges in the early morning. Few have seen it twice.
Larvitar has a tough, mossy green hide and a single horn. It is small but very heavy for its size.
Its hide is as hard as stone. It fights with stubborn courage against much bigger foes.
Pupitar's gray shell is sealed tight except for a few small holes. It sometimes shoots off without warning and crashes into things.
Inside its shell, its body is preparing for a dramatic change. It thrashes wildly when disturbed.
Tyranitar's armored body shrugs off almost any attack. Its heavy tail sweeps boulders aside as it walks.
When it stamps its feet, boulders tumble and cliffs collapse. It has little patience for weaker creatures.
Lugia's silver-white body gleams as it glides above the waves. It surfaces only rarely, and its arrival calms the sea.
Old songs in coastal villages tell of a great silver bird rising from the sea. Its cry is low and haunting.
Ho-Oh's plumage shimmers in shifting hues of red, gold and green. A single feather it drops is said to stay warm for years.
It is said to have brought three Pokémon back to life after a great fire. It roosts atop a tall tower.
Celebi drifts through time and visits peaceful woods. Its delicate wings shimmer like dew in the morning light.
Celebi is small and shy, and it vanishes in a shimmer of light when approached. Old shrines in the forest were built in its honor.
Tiny hooked pads on its feet let it cling to bark and even to smooth walls. It scampers up trunks to watch the forest floor from above.
Treecko keeps its tail raised like a small flag and swishes it to talk to others of its kind. A calm, patient hunter, it waits for insects to wander close.
Leaves along its arms are sharp enough to slice twigs clean through. It crosses the canopy in long, quiet leaps and seldom touches the ground.
Grovyle guards a stretch of woodland as its own and chases off anything that tramples the saplings. Its tail sways in time with its steps.
The seeds growing along its tail are a mark of pride, and it grooms them every morning. It moves through thick trees faster than most birds can fly.
Sceptile stands very still on a branch until prey is within reach, then strikes with the blades on its forearms. It is a fiercely loyal partner.
A warm glow lives in its belly and keeps its downy body cozy on cold nights. Hold it close and you will feel a gentle heat, like a hand warmer.
Torchic trails after whoever feeds it, peeping all the way. When startled it puffs out a few sparks, then looks quite embarrassed about it.
It trains by kicking at fence posts and stones, over and over, until the dust rises. Its legs are far stronger than its small size would suggest.
Combusken lets out a shrill cry to hearten its allies and to unsettle rivals. The feathers on its head stand up when it gets excited.
Flames burst from its wrists when it fights, and a single leap can carry it over a house. It prefers a clean, fair match against a strong opponent.
Blaziken's kicks hit with the weight of a falling beam. It grows restless if it goes too long without a worthy challenge.
The fin on its head feels the slightest change in the water and warns it of what is coming. It spends sunny afternoons dozing half buried in warm mud.
Mudkip is strong enough to heave a boulder aside with its sturdy little legs. It follows trainers around the shore, splashing in every puddle.
Its hind legs are much stronger than the front ones, so it pushes through mire with ease and stays steady where others sink.
Marshtomp likes to sit with its feet in wet soil, and it grows cranky if the ground dries out. A rainy day makes it lively and playful.
Its great arms can drag a boulder out of the way or tow a ship that has run aground. It reads the tide from the sound of the waves.
Swampert keeps a watchful eye on the shore and will carry stranded travelers back to dry land. It is happiest wading through a storm.
It will chase anything that moves, nipping at heels and tugging at cloth. A scolding makes it back off for a moment, but only a moment.
Poochyena roams in loose gangs and is bold about eating scraps left by travelers. Its ears swivel at every sound while it sniffs for a trail.
A pack follows one leader, and each member knows exactly where it stands. They herd prey together and never leave a wounded packmate behind.
Its growl is low and steady, and its stare can freeze a careless hunter in place. A trained Mightyena obeys its trainer without a bark.
It cannot walk in a straight line and weaves from side to side, nose to the ground. Anything shiny or tasty it finds goes into a hoard.
Zigzagoon rubs its back against tree trunks to leave a scent and to scratch an itch. It often trots along beside travelers for company.
Once it spots prey it dashes in a dead straight line at a speed that blurs its stripes. Turning is not its strong suit, so it often overshoots.
Linoone covers a whole meadow in a few seconds when it runs. After a hunt it flops down in the grass and naps with its legs splayed.
It chews neat crescents out of the edges of leaves, always starting at the tip. A tree full of Wurmple looks as though someone has been at it with scissors.
Wurmple sway their heads from side to side as they crawl, tasting the air for the scent of fresh growth. They hatch in spring by the hundred.
Dew beads on its pale, smooth cocoon like pearls in the morning. Birds that peck at one find the silk far tougher than it looks and soon give up.
Children count the Silcoon in a wood each spring and wait eagerly to see which of them will be the first to crack open.
Its wings carry bright eyespots that it flashes at anything that comes too close. A startled foe often freezes long enough for it to flutter away.
It drifts across meadows in loops, visiting the same flowers in the same order every day. Gardeners can set their watches by its rounds.
Its dark cocoon is rough and knobbly, blending with the bark of the tree it clings to. Woodcutters are careful to check a trunk before they swing an axe.
A Cascoon inside its shell stirs now and then, making the whole cocoon rock gently. It seems to be stretching in readiness for what comes next.
It flies only after sunset, its wings beating with a soft, papery rustle. The green dust it sheds glows faintly as it drifts down through moonlit trees.
A Dustox rests through the day pressed flat against the underside of a leaf. Its drab markings make it all but invisible among the shadows.
A wide leaf rides on top of its head and serves as a little raft, so it floats lazily across calm ponds. When the water dries up it grows weak and droopy.
Lotad sips rain from its leaf and now and then lets a drop roll off. Children like to balance it on their heads as a funny hat.
It loves to tease fishermen by tugging their lines from below, then giggling at the reaction. Its webbed hands make it a very quick swimmer.
Lombre's smooth skin is slick with a cooling film that feels pleasant on a hot day. It dislikes dry, dusty roads and stays near streams.
Cheerful music sets it dancing, and a whole group will sway and clap along together. The merrier it is, the more energy it seems to have.
Ludicolo wears a hat of broad leaves and a long, flowing fringe. It greets the morning sun with a stretch and a swaying little jig.
It hangs from a branch by the stalk on its head and looks just like an acorn. When a person walks beneath, it drops down to play a trick.
Seedot soaks up water through its feet to plump itself up, then shakes it off in a spray. It grows fussy when its shell gets dirty.
It plays a thin tune on a leaf flute at night, and the sound can unsettle travelers in the dark. It is clever and a little mischievous.
Nuzleaf's long nose wags as it sniffs for ripe berries. It shies away from crowds and watches the world from tall trees.
A single wave of its great leaf fans can whip up a gust that tosses grown people aside. It lives deep in the woods, far from any town.
Shiftry carries itself like a stern old hermit and chooses its companions with great care. Its mere shadow makes smaller creatures hush.
Brave beyond its size, it will dive at much bigger foes to defend its nest. It sulks and fluffs its feathers when it is hungry.
Taillow darts from warm lands to cool ones with the seasons. A trained one will perch on a shoulder and sing the moment it sees dawn.
It glides in wide circles, then folds its wings and drops like a stone on its target. Its glossy plumage is kept neat and spotless.
Swellow's call carries across whole valleys. It holds its head high when it lands, proud of the speed that brought it there.
It wheels over harbours crying out whenever a boat comes in. Flocks squabble loudly over anything the fishermen throw back into the water.
A Wingull sleeps floating on the waves, its head tucked beneath one wing. Rough weather barely disturbs it, since it simply rides each swell up and down.
Its bill can hold an astonishing load, and it uses it to haul home anything it fancies, from fish to driftwood. Harbour children have found lost shoes in its stash.
A Pelipper perches on harbour posts for hours, keeping a patient eye on the nets. It has learned exactly when the boats come home.
Its round head is heavy for its small body, so it often sits down to rest after a short walk. Its red horns tilt toward whatever has caught its interest.
A Ralts that is content hums so quietly that only those close by can hear it. It often falls asleep in a sunny window with its head on its arms.
Its skirt-like body flares out when it turns, and it practises slow turns for hours in empty rooms. A Kirlia that is being watched stops at once and looks elsewhere.
Kirlia grow attached to a single place where they feel safe. A Kirlia that is moved to a new home may stand by the window for days before it settles.
It moves so smoothly that its feet never seem to touch the floor, and its gown-like body barely stirs. A Gardevoir can cross a crowded room without anyone noticing.
Its arms are thin and elegant, and it uses them to sketch shapes in the air while it thinks. Those it has bonded with say they can almost read the shapes.
It skims across the surface of ponds as if on ice, never sinking. A sweet syrup oozes from its head and draws smaller creatures near.
Surskit prefers calm, clean water and will leave a pond that turns muddy. On a bright day you can see its reflection racing along beside it.
The eye patterns on its antennae look like fierce staring eyes and frighten off foes. It hovers over lakes, beating its wings to stay aloft.
Masquerain flies far out over the water in rain, its fine wings wet and shining. It folds its antennae down when it wants to rest.
It lives in damp, dark soil beneath fallen leaves and wears a cap that scatters fine spores when shaken. The cap is its pride.
Shroomish sleeps much of the day, only wandering out when the air is cool and moist. It dislikes bright sun and dry wind.
Its quick, snapping punches fall faster than the eye can follow, and its tail curls and uncurls as it strikes. It never fights without good cause.
Breloom balances on a thick springy tail, bouncing lightly from tree to tree. The cap on its head grows a bit with every year.
It hangs from a branch for most of the day and moves only a few steps before resting again. A full night's sleep is never enough for it.
Slakoth chews leaves at a snail's pace and sighs as it does. Its calm face makes an onlooker feel sleepy too.
It cannot sit still and runs about in circles, scratching at the earth and the bark. If it is made to rest it grows tense and edgy.
Vigoroth's claws leave deep marks on any tree it passes. It thrives on activity and sleeps only when it has worn itself out.
It spends its days sprawled on the ground, munching whatever is within arm's reach. When it finally stirs, the whole ground seems to shake.
Slaking is the very picture of laziness, yet one swipe of its massive arm can fell a sturdy tree. It naps until a meal comes by.
It spends long years underground, drinking from tree roots and slowly growing. Sunlight is hard on its pale eyes, so it hides in the dark.
Nincada's shell is tough but its body inside is tender. When the time is right it climbs out of the soil and cracks open.
Its wings beat so fast that its body is only a blur, and the buzz they make is deafening. Few can keep it in sight for more than a heartbeat.
Ninjask is rarely still, and it will fly all day without a pause. It is shy of crowds, and its cry rings sharply over the treetops.
A hollow shell with no breath and no pulse, it drifts about silently. People who stare too long into the dark gap of its back feel uneasy.
Shedinja does not eat or drink, and it seems to live off nothing at all. Superstitious villagers keep one far away from their homes.
Normally it speaks in a whisper, but a sudden fright makes it howl at a volume well beyond its small body. It covers its own ears when it does.
Whismur lives in quiet caves where its voice echoes. It practises squeaks and murmurs for hours and gets shy when others listen.
Heavy stamps of its feet send shock waves through the rock, and its bellow makes them stronger. A blast from its voice can rattle windows and shake pebbles loose.
Loudred listens for echoes to learn the shape of the dark places it explores. A pair of big ears stand up whenever it hears a new sound.
The tubes along its body gather air and fire it out as a roar that can be heard across a mountain. Its mouth gapes wide when it shouts.
Exploud uses different calls to signal to its friends, and a trained one can sing along with music. The sound it makes is gentle at a short range.
It slaps at tree trunks and boulders for hours to harden its palms, and it eats big meals to build up its strength. It never complains of tiredness.
Makuhita is a cheerful, stubborn fighter that gets back up every time it is thrown. It dreams of one day becoming a champion.
Its thick palms can slam with enough force to topple a truck. A bout against a human champion is a pleasure it seldom refuses.
Hariyama keeps a calm, dignified manner and trains on cold mountain slopes. It stomps the ground to settle itself before a match.
It plops down on its round tail like a cushion and rocks back and forth. An Azurill that tips over rolls about in circles, giggling all the while.
It splashes in puddles after rain and stamps until every drop has flown out. Its parents watch from nearby, ready to fish it out of deeper water.
It stands so still that minerals slowly gather on its body over the years. Cavers have chipped crystals the size of a fist from an old Nosepass.
Iron filings in the soil around it form neat lines that point to its nose. Prospectors follow these lines to find where a Nosepass is resting.
Round and round it spins after its tail, and when the world starts to swim it topples over and begins again. Anything that sways or dangles is fair game for its paws.
Skitty has a gentle purr and a bright, curious eye. Many a household keeps one because it makes such good company.
It sleeps wherever it likes and wakes only when it wants to, and no one tries to tell it otherwise. Its soft fur is groomed with great care.
Delcatty keeps to quiet corners and lets its trainer see it only at the right moments. It stalks about with its tail held high and its nose in the air.
Its gleaming eyes are really gems, and they glow in the gloom. It scrapes at cave walls for stones to eat, leaving glittering dust behind.
Sableye hides in the dark and leaps out with a grin. It is happiest in places where no light ever reaches.
The big jaws on its head are really horns shaped like a trap. It looks sweet and harmless, then snaps without warning.
Mawile smiles shyly to lure in the unwary. Behind its pleasant face is a stubborn will, and its jaws can bite through thick iron.
It eats iron ore and rails alike, and the metal builds its armor plating. Where trains run it can be found chewing the tracks.
Aron is a headstrong youngster that charges into trouble. It likes to sleep in mountain hollows with its plates tucked in.
It digs for ore in mountain slopes, and where it feeds, the ground may be left bare and scarred. Its steel hide is polished by constant rubbing on rock.
Lairon plods about with its heavy head lowered and rams anything that blocks its path. It drinks from clear mountain streams.
It defends its mountain territory fiercely, and if its armor is damaged it hurries to mend the scar with fresh ore. It tends the land it lives on.
Aggron's head and horns are mighty enough to splinter solid stone. After a landslide it clears the rubble away and plants new trees.
Snow can pile up on its head while it sits with its eyes closed, and it never brushes it off. A Meditite sneezes only once it has finished for the day.
A Meditite stretches its limbs into strange, slow poses as the sun rises. Each movement is held until its whole body trembles with effort.
It trains on narrow ledges where one wrong step would mean a long fall. A Medicham can balance on a single toe for most of an afternoon.
Medicham are said to train in pairs, each mirroring the other's movements exactly. Onlookers cannot tell which of the two is leading.
It stores energy in its fur and discharges it with a crackle when it pounces. On dry days, its mane stands up in a wild burst.
Electrike races across the plains faster than a thrown ball, sparks flickering behind it. It tires if it cannot stretch its legs.
Lightning leaps from its mane when it gets angry, and storm clouds gather above it as it runs. It darts over the fields like a flash.
Manectric's glowing mane lights up a path at night. It races ahead of storms, scouting the way for its pack.
Small sparks pop between its paws whenever it is excited. It dashes to the side of any friend in trouble and waves its arms as if to cheer them up.
Plusle's red cheeks hum with a faint charge. It loves a crowd and will jump about at a festival, dropping little static shocks on anyone who pets it.
Its blue cheeks crackle when it is in high spirits. It is shyer than its look-alike, peeking at strangers from behind its trainer's legs.
Minun hops and claps for whoever it likes, and a handful of sparks trail its fingers. Alone, it sulks quietly in a corner.
